phonemes.desc: Short open vowel [a], the first syllable of the Latin word for breath and soul.
Short [nɪ], with the vowel reduced and unstressed in Classical Latin.
Short [ma], the feminine noun ending that gives the word its grammatical form.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-nih-mah' — stress the first syllable; the middle vowel is short and light.
pronunciation.note: Anima is a Latin word, not a Greek proper name. It has no indigenous alphabetic 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form anima is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form as a scholarly citation. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath that Becomes Soul
domains.subtitle: Soul, Breath, and Life Force
domains.lead: Anima is the Latin word for breath, air, and — by extension — the soul or life-force that animates a living body. It names one of the most ancient equations in Western thought: that the difference between a corpse and a living person is the presence of breath. From this simple observation Latin developed a rich vocabulary of animation, soul, and spirit that still shapes modern psychology, religion, and biology.

cards.name: Breath
cards.desc: The literal meaning of anima: the air drawn in and expelled by living creatures.

cards.name: Soul
cards.desc: In philosophy and theology anima becomes the immaterial principle that gives life and, later, the rational soul.

cards.name: Life Force
cards.desc: The active power that distinguishes the living from the dead, the moving from the still.

cards.name: Inspiration
cards.desc: Literally 'breathing in' — the moment when life, ideas, or the divine enter the self.

symbols.name: Breath or wind
symbols.meaning: The invisible current that enters at birth and departs at death.

symbols.name: Bird
symbols.meaning: A widespread symbol for the soul as something light, winged, and capable of leaving the body.

symbols.name: Blood or pulse
symbols.meaning: The physiological sign that anima is at work in the living body.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The small fire of individual life, easily extinguished and often identified with the soul's spark.

symbols.name: The World-Soul (anima mundi)
symbols.meaning: The breath of the cosmos itself — the Stoic and Platonic doctrine that the universe is a living being, its body the world and its soul the divine air.

symbols.name: The departing breath
symbols.meaning: The final exhalation at death — the moment anima leaves the body, caught by artists as the last visible vapor of a person.

mythology.lead: Anima is not a mythological character in the Greek or Roman sense; it is a concept that acquired a long philosophical and theological history. Its 'mythology' is therefore the story of how breath became soul, and how soul became one of the foundation stones of Western psychology.

myths.title: The Breath of Life
myths.text: In Classical Latin anima first names the air itself: the breeze in the trees, the breath in the lungs. Cicero uses the word for the vital spirit that ties soul to body (Tusculanae disputationes 1), but the word's great theorist is the materialist Lucretius. In De rerum natura 3 he argues that the soul is a bodily thing — a subtle compound of heat, air, and wind, fine as smoke — dispersed and destroyed when the body dies. To understand the soul correctly, for Lucretius, is to be cured of the fear of death: no afterlife, no punishment, only rest. The Latin word thus begins as physiology and becomes philosophy in a single step. Western psychology starts here — not with a ghost in a machine, but with weather inside the body, measurable in warmth and breath.

myths.title: The Rational Soul
myths.text: Early Latin Christianity adopted anima as the standard rendering of Greek psychē, and the word's career turned theological. Tertullian devoted a treatise to it (De anima); Augustine's De quantitate animae asks, in dialogue, what the soul's 'magnitude' can be; Boethius made the soul the hinge of the Consolation of Philosophy. The scholastics completed the fusion: following Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas calls the soul the body's form — 'the first principle of life in things which live in our world' (Summa Theologiae I.75.1) — and the Council of Vienne (1312) defined as doctrine that the rational soul is truly, of itself, the form of the human body. The breath-word ended up carrying the heaviest load in Christian metaphysics, while never quite losing its breeze: between clinic and creed, anima kept both meanings at once.

myths.title: Jung's Anima
myths.text: In C. G. Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine image carried within a man's psyche — the animus its masculine counterpart in a woman. She is the soul-figure who appears in dreams, projects onto living women, mediates between the ego and the deep unconscious, and — in Jung's phrase — is 'the archetype of life itself' (Aion, CW 9ii). His early formulation (The Relations between the Ego and the Unconscious, 1928) treats her as the very function through which a man experiences his own soul. The ancient equation survives intact under the new terminology: the soul is still made of air, but now the air is what moves between two people — the atmosphere of feeling and relationship that modern psychology learned to study by giving it her old Latin name.

myths.title: Animation and Life
myths.text: The descendants of anima form a genealogy of the living. An animal is a being that breathes; to animate is to put breath into matter; animation is the craft of giving apparent life to drawings; animism is the ascription of soul to rivers, trees, and stones; equanimity is an even soul; unanimity is many spirits agreeing as one. Each English word preserves a different inflection of the Latin root, and each still points back to breath. Two thousand years after Lucretius dispersed the soul into wind, every cartoon that moves, every creature that breathes, and every argument that matter itself might be alive still testifies to the old insight the word was coined to hold: that the difference between living and dead is the presence of something as invisible, and as real, as air.

lore.syncretism: The Latin anima overlaps with Greek psychē, Hebrew nephesh, Sanskrit ātman, and Greek pneuma. All of these terms begin with breath or wind and develop into concepts of soul, spirit, or self. In medieval philosophy anima became the bridge between Aristotelian biology and Christian theology, a development that shaped European thought until the early modern period. In modern psychology it survives as Jung's anima and as the root of 'animation,' the art of giving apparent life to images.
lore.culturalLegacy: Anima is one of the most quietly influential words in Western languages. It underlies 'animal' (a being that has breath), 'animate' (to give life), 'animation' (the illusion of life in images), and 'animism' (the attribution of soul to natural objects). In Jungian psychology the anima is a central archetype, and in contemporary spirituality it names the feminine soul-principle. The word's persistence shows that the ancient equation of breath with life has never really been replaced.
lore.extendedMeditation:
To meditate on Anima is to meditate on the boundary between body and whatever we call the self. Breath is the one physiological process that can be voluntary or automatic; it links the conscious will to the autonomic body. The Latin word reminds us that the soul was not originally imagined as a ghost in a machine but as the very fact of being alive.

In a digital age, when consciousness is often modelled as computation, Anima asks a simpler question: what is it that makes a living thing living? The answer may not be a substance but a process — the continuous exchange of inner and outer, self and world, that breath so perfectly symbolizes.
lore.originalScriptNote: Anima is a Latin word. It has no 'original script' in the sense of Greek or cuneiform; its canonical form is the Latin spelling anima. The ASCII form anima already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Anima is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Scholarly Transliteration' or simply 'Latin'.

lore.archaeology: A concept has no tombs, but it has manuscripts, and the material trail of anima is among the most dramatic in Latin literature. Lucretius' De rerum natura — the greatest ancient book of the soul's materiality — survives through a single early medieval lineage, crowned by the ninth-century codex Oblongus (Leiden, Bibliotheek der Rijksuniversiteit, Vossianus Latinus F 30); the poem's recovery in 1417, when Poggio Bracciolini's agents pulled a copy from a German monastery shelf, detonated the Renaissance debate over atom and soul. Augustine's De quantitate animae and the scholastic summae travelled in hundreds of copies across medieval Europe. Jung's twentieth-century revival rests on printed editions and the working library at Küsnacht — archaeology of a different kind.
